title: Better Than Average Drivers
text:
In a short study published in 1981, the Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson asked groups of students in the United States and in Sweden a simple question: compared with the other people in this room, how skillful and how safe a driver are you?

Participants placed themselves on a scale by percentage, from the least skilled to the most skilled in the group. By definition, only half of any group can be above the median. Yet in the American group about 93 percent rated themselves as more skillful than the median driver, and about 88 percent rated themselves as safer. The Swedish students were more modest but still far from the logical limit: around 69 percent rated their skill above the median, and about 77 percent their safety.

The result became one of the best known illustrations of the better-than-average effect, a form of overconfidence in which most people believe they are above average in abilities they value. Later studies found similar patterns for many skills and traits, from getting along with others to ethics. They also found the effect is strongest for vague, self-defined qualities, where each person can define "good driving" in terms of what they happen to do well, and weaker for concrete, measurable skills.

Svenson noted that such self-assessments can make people feel less need for caution than their actual driving warrants.
lesson: If you feel sure you are better than most at something, look for objective feedback before relying on that feeling, especially where an error can hurt you or others.
source: Svenson, O. (1981). Are we all less risky and more skillful than our fellow drivers? Acta Psychologica, 47(2), 143-148.
caveat: The sample was small (students only), though the better-than-average effect has been found widely since.
